charts.revenue_profit_tooltip: This chart illustrates the company's operational efficiency. <1>Revenue</1> indicates sales volume, <2>EBITDA</2> reflects operating profitability, and <3>Net Income</3> represents the bottom-line result. An investor looks for a consistent growth trajectory across all three metrics, where profitability (EBITDA/Income) matches or outpaces sales growth.
charts.revenue_profit_subtitle: Business Evolution: Revenue vs EBITDA vs Net Income
charts.margins_tooltip: This chart reveals how efficiently the company retains money at each stage of the business. <1>Gross Margin</1> is the profit remaining after direct production costs. <2>Operating Margin</2> also deducts day-to-day business expenses. <3>Net Margin</3> is the true percentage left at the end. An investor looks for stability or expansion in these margins, which demonstrates pricing power and cost control.
charts.roce_wacc_tooltip: This is perhaps the most critical chart for evaluating value destruction. <1>ROCE</1> is the return the company extracts from its investments. <2>WACC</2> is the cost it paid to borrow that money (interest). If the ROCE bar is consistently higher than WACC, the company creates wealth; if it's lower, it is literally burning cash.
charts.cashflow_capex_tooltip: This chart focuses on capital intensity. <1>CapEx</1> (Capital Expenditures) is the money required to maintain or expand the business. It is subtracted from <2>Operating Cash Flow</2> to arrive at the final <3>Free Cash Flow</3>. A highly capital-intensive company requires most of its operating cash flow to be consumed by CapEx, leaving little free cash.
charts.shares_tooltip: This chart shows the total number of <1>shares outstanding</1>. If the line is falling, the company is buying back its own stock (Buybacks), which is excellent for investors because each remaining share represents a larger slice of the profits. If the line is rising, the company is issuing new stock (Dilution), which decreases the value of existing shareholders' stakes.
charts.liquidity_profile_tooltip: This chart focuses on short-term survival. <1>Current Assets</1> are cash or assets convertible to cash within a year. <2>Current Liabilities</2> are debts due within a year. The <3>Current Ratio</3> divides the two: if it's above 1.0x, the company can comfortably pay its short-term obligations.
charts.debt_profile_tooltip: Here we analyze debt health. <1>Total Debt</1> is compared against <2>Cash & Equivalents</2> to see if the company has liquidity to pay what it owes. The <3>Debt/EBITDA</3> line estimates how many years it would take to pay off the debt using current operating profits. Values below 3x are generally considered safe.
charts.earnings_quality_tooltip: This chart reveals the true quality of the company's earnings. <1>Net Income</1> is the accounting profit on 'paper', while <2>Free Cash Flow</2> is the actual cash that entered the bank account. An investor expects these two metrics to move closely together. If a company reports record profits but cash flow is consistently low or negative, it's a major red flag.
charts.earnings_quality_subtitle: Net Income vs Free Cash Flow
charts.opex_breakdown_tooltip: This chart breaks down the company's operating costs. <1>R&D</1> represents investment in innovation and new products (the engine of future growth). <2>SG&A</2> covers fixed costs for sales, marketing, and administration (the cost of keeping the lights on). An investor looks for companies that keep SG&A controlled relative to revenue, and depending on the sector (e.g., Tech), a strong and continuous investment in R&D.
charts.eps_tooltip: The <1>Diluted EPS</1> (Earnings Per Share) indicates how much profit the company generated for each outstanding share. The word 'Diluted' means it already accounts for the most conservative scenario: assuming all employee stock options and convertible bonds have been transformed into actual shares. An investor focuses on this metric because it represents the exact slice of profit that belongs to each share in their portfolio.
charts.capital_structure_tooltip: This chart illustrates how the company finances its operations. <1>Total Equity</1> represents shareholders' money and retained earnings, while <2>Total Liabilities</2> represents debts and obligations. Investors look for companies with a healthy proportion, where debt doesn't overwhelm equity, ensuring long-term financial solidity.
charts.working_capital_tooltip: Working Capital shows the money 'tied up' in daily operations. <1>Accounts Receivable</1> is money customers still owe the company, and <2>Inventory</2> are products in the warehouse. In contrast, <3>Accounts Payable</3> is money the company still owes suppliers. An investor wants to see the company collecting cash fast, keeping low inventory, and stretching terms with suppliers.
charts.fcf_conversion_tooltip: FCF Conversion measures what percentage of <1>Net Income</1> (Accounting Profit) is actually converted into hard cash. <2>Operating Cash Flow</2> is the cash generated by operations, and <3>Free Cash Flow</3> is what remains after essential investments. An excellent company consistently converts its profit into cash; frequent divergences are a major red flag.
charts.shareholder_returns_tooltip: This chart shows how the company returns value directly to shareholders. It can be done in two ways: paying <1>Dividends Paid</1> (cash in your account) or through <2>Stock Repurchases</2> (buying back shares, which makes your remaining shares worth more). Investors love seeing these two bars grow sustainably over time.
charts.cash_flow_pillars_tooltip: The 3 pillars of cash flow explain how money moves: <1>Operating Cash Flow</1> (money the core business generates), <2>Investing Cash Flow</2> (money spent or received from buying/selling assets), and <3>Financing Cash Flow</3> (money from loans, dividends, or new stock). Ideally, you want to see operations generating plenty of cash to support investments.
charts.valuation_multiples_tooltip: This chart compares two essential market multiples. <1>EV/EBITDA</1> values the entire enterprise (independent of debt or taxes), while <2>P/E</2> focuses exclusively on shareholder earnings. An investor looks for stability or contraction in these multiples over time, which indicates the company is becoming cheaper relative to its ability to generate results.
charts.earnings_cashflow_multiples_tooltip: This chart compares how much the market is willing to pay for each dollar of earnings versus each dollar of actual cash generated. The <1>P/E Ratio</1> is based on accounting profit, while the <2>P/FCF Ratio</2> is based on actual cash that came in. A P/FCF much higher than P/E might indicate that earnings aren't translating to cash flow, warranting caution.
charts.roe_roic_tooltip: Here we evaluate management's competence. <1>Return on Equity</1> (ROE) measures profit generated solely with shareholders' money, which can be artificially inflated by debt. <2>Return on Capital Employed</2> (ROIC) is stricter: it measures efficiency in generating profit using all capital (including debt). Outstanding companies have consistently high ROIC.
charts.fcf_yield_tooltip: The <1>FCF Yield</1> acts like the theoretical 'interest rate' on your investment if the company paid you all its leftover cash. It's calculated by dividing Free Cash Flow by the total market value of the company (Market Cap). Higher values generally indicate the stock is cheaper and more attractive (like buying a rental property with a higher yield).
charts.leverage_ratio_tooltip: <1>Debt to Equity</1> assesses financial risk. It compares total debt to shareholders' money (Equity). High values (above 2.0x) mean the company relies much more on debt than on its own money, making it vulnerable in a crisis. A value below 1.0x is generally a sign of great safety.

valuation.matrix_help_desc: The matrix shows how the valuation changes if our growth and risk assumptions are slightly wrong. A mostly green matrix indicates a high margin of safety—the investment remains profitable even if the economy worsens. A mostly red matrix warns that the investment is highly speculative.
valuation.matrix_subtitle: Intrinsic value per share based on variations in WACC (Y-axis) and Terminal Growth Rate (X-axis).
valuation.cashflows_subtitle: Projected Free Cash Flow for the next 10 years (in Billions USD).
valuation.tooltip_growth_1_5: Estimated annual Free Cash Flow growth for the first 5 years.
valuation.tooltip_growth_6_10: Estimated annual Free Cash Flow growth from year 6 to 10.
valuation.tooltip_wacc: Weighted Average Cost of Capital. Represents the risk and required rate of return.
valuation.tooltip_terminal: Expected perpetual growth rate for the company after year 10.
valuation.negative_fcf_error_desc: This company currently has a negative Free Cash Flow. The classic DCF model applies growth rates to the base FCF, meaning negative cash flows will mathematically "grow" larger into the future. Therefore, a DCF valuation is fundamentally incompatible with this company at its current stage.
